title: The parliament of observers - Against the observable axiom of quantum mechanics
abstract: The 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences' may at times give the impression that natural science, especially modern theoretical physics, is all but a formal apparatus. However, a key challenge of physics remains to align everyday notions of experience -- be it directly or mediated through instruments of arbitrary sophistication -- with their mathematical formalisation. This applies in particular to quantum theory, arguably the most successful theory of physics ever invented. One of its core assumptions postulates: $Observables\ correspond\ with\ self-adjoint\ operators.$ Here, we argue that already this most basic premise about the quantum formalism falls apart under careful scrutiny, at least when understood for all observables at once. In other words, we challenge the role of the noncommutative algebra of bounded operators as an adequate formalisation of the 'algebra of observables', understood as (equivalence classes of) measurement procedures that admit a coherent empirical interpretation.
summary: This paper critically re-examines the foundational axiom linking physical observables to self-adjoint operators in quantum mechanics. By developing a minimal formal definition of an observable based on experimental contexts, the authors demonstrate that this fundamental correspondence breaks down under rigorous scrutiny. It prompts a re-evaluation of the mathematical structure underpinning quantum theory itself.
main_problem: The paper fundamentally challenges the core axiom of quantum mechanics stating that every observable corresponds to a self-adjoint operator, arguing this premise fails when considering all observables simultaneously.
main_result: The authors argue that a basic consistency requirement derived from the concept of 'observables' (as measurement procedures) is mathematically incompatible with the structure of the algebra of self-adjoint operators.
method: The approach involves developing a minimal, context-independent formal definition of an observable based on experimental contexts and then deriving necessary algebraic consistency conditions.
model_or_system: The analysis is general, focusing on the formal structure of quantum systems ($S$) and the abstract concept of an 'observable' defined by its measurement context, rather than a specific Hamiltonian or physical realization.
key_observables: Observables are defined conceptually as 'equivalence classes of measurement procedures' or bounded, measurable functions on outcome spaces.
important_parameters: The analysis considers the transition from Projection-Valued Measures (PVMs) to general Positive Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs).
main_assumptions: The initial framework assumes that observables can be characterized by an underlying, consistent set of experimental contexts, and the analysis proceeds by identifying redundancies via 'operational indistinguishability'.
figures_summary: Figure 1 is noted to deconstruct the quantum-mechanical correspondence rule, illustrating the relationship between physical measurements and the mathematical abstraction to self-adjoint operators.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the problematic axiom, then developing a minimal formalization of observables based on experimental contexts, and finally showing that the consistency requirements of this minimal model conflict with the structure of the standard operator algebra.
why_interesting: This work directly challenges the foundational axioms of quantum theory, which is crucial for any theoretical physicist working on open quantum systems or interpreting measurement processes.
